items.text: Passage 1: You must enter the characters with black color that stand out from the other characters NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Message: * A friend wanted you to see this item from WRAL.com: http://wr.al/1755W NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR ? A quick-thinking Johnston County emergency dispatcher is credited with saving the day after he helped police locate a woman who was trapped inside the trunk of a car. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR On Jan. 14, 911 supervisor Tim Medlin received a call from a woman who said she was locked in the trunk of a moving car by her jealous boyfriend. Medlin said it was hard to understand her. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "The only thing we knew is it was a female that was very upset, and that she was in the trunk of the car," he said. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The call got disconnected. He called back but could not reach the woman. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Medlin then had the idea to text her from a cell phone. She responded. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "Texting, it was the only way I knew we would probably not get her in trouble," Medlin said. "When I sent a simple text, 'Can you text?' She responded, 'Yes.' The immediate response after that was, 'Help me.'" NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The woman was able to provide Medlin with the make and color of the vehicle and told him she believed she was headed to Fayetteville. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Medlin called the Cumberland County Sheriff's office, who then contacted Verizon Wireless, and was able to locate the phone. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The woman also gave authorities the name of her boyfriend - Nicholas Mattevi. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Once they had a location, Fayetteville police spotted the car, rescued the woman and arrested Mattevi. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "They located her. It was a good feeling to know she was located," Medlin said. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Jason Barbour, Johnston County's 911 director, said all 911 centers can receive text messages, but cannot initiate them, something he says needs to change. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "This is a prime example of technology being used to the fullest at someone's greatest time of need," Barbour said. "We can only receive texts and then text back one another. We can't start the conversation. So that was the problem." NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Barbour said he is glad Medlin had a cell phone nearby to text the woman, but believes all 911 centers should be able to be updated so that they can initiate texts from their systems. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Mattevi was charged with false imprisonment. He was released on a $10,000 bond. Passage 2: A 911 dispatcher for Johnston County, North Carolina, recently helped save a woman who was locked in the trunk of a moving car, according to officials. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The 29-year-old woman called 911 around 4 a.m. on Jan. 14, 2017, saying she had a disagreement with her boyfriend, who forced her into a trunk, Jason Barbour, director of the Johnston County Emergency 911 Communications Center, said. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Barbour told ABC News today that the shift supervisor at the time, Tim Medlin, responded to the call. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "She was crying and very upset, so it was hard to understand her at first, but [Medlin] finally heard her say she was locked in a trunk of a car," Barbour explained. "The call then dropped, and his multiple attempts to call her back were unsuccessful." NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Medlin "refused to give up" and used the office's emergency cellphone in an attempt to reach the woman, according to Barbour. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "It was this flip phone, and [Medlin] texted the woman on that phone since he couldn't reach her by calling," Barbour said. "Fortunately, she started texting back and told us that she needed help and that she believed she was in a red Mustang headed towards Fayetteville." NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Medlin was then able to get the woman's location with the help of a cellphone provider. Police responded and stopped the car in the city of Fayetteville, Barbour said. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "And lo and behold, the woman was in the trunk of the car," Barbour said. He added that if it wasn't for Medlin's quick thinking, the woman may not have been found on time. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "He really stood by our motto, 'Failure is not an option,'" Barbour said. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Lt. Todd Joyce, a public information officer for the Fayetteville Police Department, told ABC News today that the woman in the trunk was found unharmed. He added that her boyfriend, 32-year-old Nicholas Mattevi, was arrested around 5 a.m. and charged with false imprisonment, a misdemeanor. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Fayetteville Police Department NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Mattevi has since been released from jail, according to Joyce. He said it was not immediately clear if Mattevi had obtained a lawyer or entered a plea. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR ABC News could not reach Mattevi for comment. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The Cumberland County District Court did not immediately respond to ABC News' request for information. Passage 3: A 911 dispatcher's quick thinking may have saved a life or prevented a more serious crime. It happened in Johnston County as a woman was locked in the trunk of car going down the interstate.Around 4 a.m. Saturday, January 14, Johnston County 911 Shift Supervisor Tim Medlin got a 911 cell phone call from a woman who said she'd been kidnapped from Raleigh and put in the trunk of a car which was traveling down the highway.At that point, the car was headed east on I-40 nearing the I-95 interchange. Dispatchers had that information from a cell phone tracking device. But, the caller wasn't able to tell dispatchers anything else valuable before the call was lost.She didn't answer when they called back. That's when Medlin had an idea. Dispatchers had a cell phone to notify supervisors if the land lines went out. He decided to use it to text the woman who called.She responded, told them she knew the man driving, and were likely headed to Fayetteville. Dispatchers sent Fayetteville police to the address. They arrested Nicholas Mattevi and charged him with false imprisonment.There was huge sigh of relief in the Johnston County 911 center."Okay, they're out with her. They've got them. They've confirmed that they've got them. We're like, 'Okay, this is over with. It's done. I can go home. I can go to bed. We've done our job,'" Medlin recalled.The phone that Medlin used is an old flip phone. His boss told ABC11 Monday he's going to buy a smart phone for the team so if it ever happens again they'll have a keyboard.

items.text: Passage 1: CLOSE Vanderbilt Chancellor Nicholas S. Zeppos discusses why the university is renaming Confederate Memorial Hall. Vanderbilt University NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Buy Photo Workers cover up the name on the exterior of Confederate Memorial Hall at Vanderbilt University on Monday, Aug. 15, 2016. Vanderbilt will repay an 83-year-old donation, allowing it to remove the Confederate name from the residence hall. (Photo: Andrew Nelles / The Tennessean)Buy Photo Story Highlights Confederate Memorial Hall opened 1935 with support from United Daughters of the Confederacy. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Vanderbilt first sought to change the name in 2002. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Starting in 2005, the university began referring to the building as Memorial Hall. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR To change the name, Vanderbilt raised $1.2 million to repay the United Daughters of the Confederacy. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Vanderbilt University will repay an 83-year-old donation in order to remove from a residence hall what its leader called "a symbol and a reminder of racism, slavery and a very, very bloody Civil War." NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Chancellor Nicholas S. Zeppos made the announcement Monday, capping a 14-year effort to rename Confederate Memorial Hall. The building, which has had that name etched into the stone above its entrance since it opened in 1935, stands in the heart of the university's freshman commons, and has frequently spurred debate about the university's attitude toward an increasingly diverse student body. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR In an interview with The Tennessean, Zeppos ? who arrived on campus as a law professor in 1987 ? said he had long been in favor of changing the building's name. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "It's a symbol that is, for many people, deeply offensive and painful," Zeppos said in the interview. "And to walk past it or to have to live in that space is really something that I just don't think is acceptable." NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The United Daughters of the Confederacy originally donated $50,000 in 1933 toward the building?s construction and naming rights in order to honor Confederate soldiers who died during the Civil War. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Vanderbilt previously attempted to rename the building Memorial Hall in 2002, but the Tennessee Division of the United Daughters of the Confederacy sued to keep the original name. A Tennessee appeals court ruled in 2005 that Vanderbilt could remove ?Confederate? from the inscription only after it had returned the donation at its current value. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Anonymous donors recently gave the university the $1.2 million needed for that purpose; the Vanderbilt Board of Trust authorized the move this summer. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Doug Jones, the Nashville attorney who represented the Daughters of the Confederacy against Vanderbilt, called the move "a real slam on the history of our country." NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR ?All it was was just a simple monument for the boys in Tennessee that died? in the Civil War, Jones said, adding that the name was not connected with slavery. ?We think rewriting history?s just terrible. And I think it?s a very sad day for a school with that kind of reputation to be condoning that." NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Universities across the country have faced similar decisions as they re-evaluated the implications of their buildings' names. Students and officials at Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro have spent months pushing to remove the name of Nathan Bedford Forrest, a founder of the Ku Klux Klan, from a campus building. MTSU and the Tennessee Board of Regents approved the change, which now goes before a state panel. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Zeppos flatly rebuffed the criticism that changing the name of a residence hall would compromise the university's approach to its long and complicated history. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "We are not saying this is not part of Vanderbilt's history," he said. "I think we teach history by how we talk about these events. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "I don't think that that (name) was really teaching anyone history." NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The longstanding effort to rename the residence hall took on renewed urgency over the past couple of years, as universities across Tennessee and the country grappled with the shadow of racism and slavery on their campuses. At Vanderbilt, founded in 1873 just eight years after the Civil War ended, the name change follows a series of changes made over the past year to address diversity, including the addition of a chief diversity officer to the university's leadership team. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR In 2005, Vanderbilt officially began referring to the building as Memorial Hall, although the word Confederate remained on its facade. Students, faculty and high-ranking administrators argued passionately to remove the word at a town hall on the subject last fall. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Ariana Fowler, president of Vanderbilt Student Government, praised the university leadership for the decision to formally rename the residence hall. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR ?This action demonstrates the administration's attentiveness to student needs and concerns, as well as sets a great precedent for advocating on behalf of those who may feel marginalized on our campus,? Fowler said in the university statement. ?This is an excellent next step in the direction of becoming an institution that not only admits diverse students, but ensures their care and support ? one who is eager to eliminate any barriers that may stand in the way of such a goal.? NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Zeppos said the decision to remove the mention of the Confederacy from the building spoke to the courage of students, faculty and staff who spoke out against it for years. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "I hope that they feel as if they've made a big difference in Vanderbilt and in Vanderbilt's history themselves," he said. "It hopefully says we have listened, we have made changes. But I don't think we should assume that our work is completed in any way." NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Crews were already working Monday night to cover the name over the building?s entrance. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Reach Adam Tamburin at 615-726-5986 and on Twitter @tamburintweets. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Vanderbilt University began referring to Confederate Memorial Hall as Memorial Hall in 2005. The year was wrong in an earlier version of this story.? NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Around the nation NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR CLOSE The Southern Baptist Convention voted to urge its congregations to stop displaying Confederate flags. The church is by far the largest in the South.Video provided by Newsy Newslook NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR &amp;amp;amp;nbsp; &amp;amp;amp;nbsp; &amp;amp;amp;lt;!--iframe--&amp;amp;amp;gt; &amp;amp;amp;nbsp; NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Read or Share this story: http://tnne.ws/2bkJwgO Passage 2: FILE - This Sept. 30, 2003, file photo, shows the exterior of a dormitory at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tenn., is inscribed with the name Confederate Memorial Hall. The private university announced... (Associated Press) NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR FILE - This Sept. 30, 2003, file photo, shows the exterior of a dormitory at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tenn., is inscribed with the name Confederate Memorial Hall. The private university announced on Monday, Aug. 15, 2016, that it has struck an agreement to pay $1.2 million to United Daughters... (Associated Press) NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR FILE - This Sept. 30, 2003, file photo, shows the exterior of a dormitory at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tenn., is inscribed with the name Confederate Memorial Hall. The private university announced on Monday, Aug. 15, 2016, that it has struck an agreement to pay $1.2 million to United Daughters... (Associated Press) FILE - This Sept. 30, 2003, file photo, shows the exterior of a dormitory at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tenn., is inscribed with the name Confederate Memorial Hall. The private university announced... (Associated Press) NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) ? Vanderbilt University announced Monday that it will pay more than a million dollars to remove an inscription containing the word "Confederate" from one of its campus dorms. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The private university has referred to the Confederate Memorial Hall simply as "Memorial Hall" since 2002, but was blocked in court from changing the name chiseled on the building because it was constructed with the help of a $50,000 gift from the United Daughters of the Confederacy in 1933. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Under the agreement, Vanderbilt will pay $1.2 million, the equivalent of the gift made 83 years ago, to the organization's Tennessee chapter. In exchange, the chapter will relinquish its naming rights to the building. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "You can memorialize individuals without taking sides in the bloodiest war that was fought over the divisive issues of slavery and equality that we're still struggling with today for those young people coming onto campus," Vanderbilt Chancellor Nicholas Zeppos said in a phone interview. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The money has been pledged by anonymous donors, and Zeppos said the school chooses to focus on "moving Vanderbilt forward" rather than on what projects the Daughters of the Confederacy will spend the funds on, especially in light of a new Tennessee law that makes it more difficult to remove Confederate symbols and statues from public places. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR "The donors and I and others understand that this donation will go to another organization, but this is a very positive step for Vanderbilt," Zeppos said. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The Daughters of the Confederacy did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR About 30 miles to the southeast, Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro wants to remove the name of Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest from one of its buildings. The public higher education system overseeing the school endorsed the change last month, but the proposal faces a tougher hurdle when it reaches the Tennessee Historical Commission. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Under the "Tennessee Heritage Protection Act" passed earlier this year, it now takes a vote of at least two-thirds of the commission to approve changing or removing historical markers. That's an increase from the previous requirement of a simple majority vote. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Calls to remove Confederate imagery from public places multiplied across the South after last year's slaying of nine black churchgoers in Charleston, South Carolina. A white man espousing racist views and who posed in a photo with a Confederate flag has been charged with murder in the killings. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Following the church shooting, Republican Gov. Bill Haslam said he supported removing the Capitol bust of Forrest, who is famous for his exploits as a Confederate cavalry general and amassed a fortune as a plantation owner and slave trader in Memphis before the Civil War. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR After the defeat of the Confederacy, the newly formed Ku Klux Klan elected Forrest its honorary grand wizard, though he publicly denied being involved. Two years later, he ordered the Klan to disband because of its members' increasing violence. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR The Forrest bust remains in the lobby between the House and Senate chambers at the state Capitol.
